questions.q: In the lesson's original `run_bell_experiment()` example, what three responsibilities are glued together in one function?
options: Importing, printing, and returning
Building the circuit, deciding which backend to run on, and deciding the shot count
Testing, documenting, and deploying
Encrypting, transmitting, and decrypting results
questions.explain: The original function mixes circuit construction, backend selection, and shot-count decisions into a single function body, with no way to change any one of them independently of the others.

questions.q: Why can't `run_bell_experiment()` as originally written be unit-tested the way Lesson 6's construction tests work?
options: Because Qiskit circuits can never be tested
Because building the circuit and running it on AerSimulator happen in the same function, so testing the circuit's structure would require actually instantiating and running a backend
Because the function doesn't return anything
Because pytest cannot import functions that use AerSimulator
questions.explain: Since construction and execution are fused together, there's no way to isolate and test just the circuit-building logic without also triggering a backend run -- defeating the purpose of a fast, deterministic construction test.

questions.q: What does the dependency-injection fix in this lesson mean specifically, applied to a quantum backend?
options: Having the circuit-construction function import and instantiate the backend internally
Passing the backend into the execution function as a parameter, rather than the function constructing or importing it internally
Hardcoding the backend name as a string constant at the top of the module
Removing the backend entirely and always using a statevector
questions.explain: Dependency injection means run_circuit(circuit, backend, shots) receives the backend as a parameter from its caller, instead of reaching out to construct an AerSimulator (or any other backend) internally.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say a default backend parameter pointing at real hardware is risky, recommending `None` (forcing an explicit choice) instead?
options: Because None is required syntax in Python function signatures
Because a hidden default could silently submit jobs to real hardware (with real queue time and cost) when a caller expected a local simulator
Because real hardware backends cannot be passed as parameters
Because AerSimulator does not support default arguments
questions.explain: A hidden default pointing at real hardware risks a caller unintentionally submitting to a real device -- forcing the caller to explicitly supply a backend (with no implicit real-hardware default) avoids that silent risk.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say this construction/execution separation is a prerequisite for the backend-abstraction pattern covered in Lesson 11, rather than just a nice-to-have?
options: It isn't actually required for Lesson 11's pattern
Backend abstraction formalizes the 'backend' parameter into a shared interface, which only makes sense once circuit code no longer hardcodes or imports a specific backend itself
Lesson 11's pattern only works with Q#, not Qiskit
Backend abstraction requires circuits to never be tested
questions.explain: Backend abstraction (Lesson 11) formalizes the backend parameter into a shared interface so swapping implementations requires changing one argument. That's only possible once circuit-construction code has already been decoupled from any specific backend, which is exactly this lesson's refactor.
